core: the working definition of a one-to-one relationship: each row in the first table can match at most one row in the second table, and each row in the second can match at most one row in the first
when one-to-one is used: deliberately splitting one table into two for security or size, with user accounts and user profiles as the classic example
how one-to-one is implemented: a foreign key with a uniqueness rule on the linking column, so neither side can repeat
one-to-one versus one-to-many, using a person and their passport versus a customer and their orders
why one-to-one is rare: most real relationships are one-to-many
the rule of thumb: if two tables are always one-to-one, they might be one table
supporting: one-to-one is documented as uncommon and often a sign of redundant data or a suboptimal design
the unique constraint is the documented mechanism for forbidding repeated values in a column
a foreign key by itself allows repeats; the uniqueness rule is what turns a link into a one-to-one link
splitting a table can keep sensitive login data apart from general profile data
outOfScope: relationships as a general concept (own topic: databases-and-sql:foundations:relationships)
SQL syntax for keys and constraints (own topics: sql-basics and the SQL family)

claims.claim: A one-to-one relationship means each row in the first table can match at most one row in the second table, and each row in the second can match at most one row in the first.

One-to-one is uncommon in practice; database documentation describes it as a cardinality type that is not common and likely represents a suboptimal model design because of the storage of redundant data.
A one-to-one relationship can be created when both tables each contain a column of common and unique values, meaning neither linking column may hold a repeated value.

A foreign key is a column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table; on its own it allows repeated values, so a uniqueness rule is what limits a link to at most one match on each side.

One-to-one is mostly used to split a table in two in order to provide information concisely and make it more understandable, and a single business entity can be stored as two tables when its data comes from different sources.
In a one-to-many relationship the 'one' side column holds unique values while the 'many' side column may contain duplicates; a customer and their orders is the standard shape of this relationship.

Design guidance recommends consolidating two one-to-one related tables into a single table when possible, because keeping them separate adds clutter and produces unexpected results when rows do not match on both sides.

conflictingEvidence.issue: No single documentation source states the working definition verbatim as 'at most one on each side'.
positions: Microsoft Learn's Power BI documentation expresses one-to-one as 'both columns contain unique values' and lists the cardinality shorthand 1:1.
Wikipedia's data-modeling article defines cardinality as the numerical relationship between rows of one table and rows in another and lists one-to-one among the common cardinalities.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the at-most-one-on-each-side phrasing as the working definition synthesized across documentation, and attributes its two parts separately (both columns unique; numerical relationship between rows).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Design advice about splitting versus merging one-to-one tables points in both directions.
positions: Wikipedia frames a one-to-one split as useful: 'mostly used to split a table in two in order to provide information concisely and make it more understandable'.
Microsoft Learn's one-to-one guidance recommends 'consolidating the data into a single model table' and avoiding one-to-one relationships that span tables.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reconciles the two: a split is justified when there is a real reason (sensitive data, optional columns, data from different sources); otherwise the rule of thumb applies — two tables that are always one-to-one might be one table.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The classic user-accounts-and-user-profiles example is a textbook pattern, not a documented definition.
positions: The split-for-security motivation follows from the documented reasons to separate data (Wikipedia's split-a-table rationale; Microsoft Learn's row-data-spans-across-tables scenario).
No researched source uses the exact accounts/profiles example.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The accounts/profiles example is presented as an original illustration of the documented split pattern, and the security motivation is recorded as an INTERPRETIVE claim grounded in those documented premises.
